sections.facts: The Gujarat Panchayat Act, 1961 came into force on June 15, 1962 in the State of Gujarat except in the Kutch area and the district of Dangs. On March 4, 1963, areas within the jurisdiction of several municipalities constituted under the Bombay Municipal Act, 1901 were declared to be gram or nagar, and sections 203 to 205 were brought into operation on April 1, 1963. The State Government entrusted land revenue recovery functions and delegated powers under the Land Revenue Code to nagar and gram panchayats, and promulgated various service rules including Conduct, Discipline & Appeal, Absorption Seniority, Pay & Allowances, Transfer, Promotion, and Pension Rules. On January 2, 1967, an order was passed under section 203(2) directing that the Panchayat Service consist of district, taluka, and local cadres, specifying local cadre posts in Part III of the Schedule. However, the State Government did not make any order regarding equation of posts or pay scale fixation for local cadre staff till 1975 despite repeated representations, nor framed promotional rules, nor extended the pay revision benefits recommended by the First Pay Commission (Sarela Commission) and Second Pay Commission (Desai Commission). Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 filed a representative writ application seeking equivalence of posts, fixation of seniority, pay scales and allowances with retrospective effect and arrears, framing of promotional avenue rules, and retrospective extension of the pay revision benefits. Following its earlier decision in G. L. Shukla v. State of Gujarat, the High Court held that respondents in the local cadre were government servants and allowed the application. During the State's appeal, the Gujarat Panchayats (Amendment) Ordinance, 1978 was promulgated and replaced by the Gujarat Panchayats (Third Amendment) Act, 1978, leading the employees to file writ petitions challenging the Amending Act.
sections.statute: Gujarat Panchayats Act, 1961 (Gujarat Act No. VI of 1962), Sections 102, 122, 142, 143(2)(c), 149, 157, 158, 203, 205, 206, 207, 210, 325; Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901; Land Revenue Code; Gujarat Panchayats (Amendment) Ordinance, 1978; Gujarat Panchayats (Third Amendment) Act, 1978; Constitution of India, Articles 12, 40, 162, 276, 277, 309, 310, Part XIV, Seventh Schedule (List I, Entry 70; List II, Entries 5 and 41).
sections.argument: It was contended by the petitioners that the Panchayat Service was as much a service under the State as any other Civil Service; that the State Government had failed to discharge its statutory duties in relation to the members of the staff included in the local cadre of the Panchayat Service; and that the denial of benefits similar to those extended to other members of the State Civil Service on the basis of the reports of the two Pay Commissions amounted to hostile discrimination. The State Government contested the application, alleging that the members of the Panchayat Service were not government servants.
sections.analysis: The true test for determining whether a person holds a civil post or is a member of a civil service is the existence of a master-servant relationship between the State and the person holding the post, indicated by the State's right to select and appoint, suspend and dismiss, control the manner and method of doing work, and pay wages or remuneration (State of Assam v. Nanak Chandra Dutta; Superintendent of Post Offices v. P. K. Rajamma). In local bodies, officers drawn from provincial or State services and deputed to local bodies retained their identity as State Civil Service officers even if paid by local bodies, as they discharged legitimate governmental functions decentralised to foster democracy. Part XIV and Articles 309 and 310 of the Constitution treat persons holding civil posts under a State as persons serving the State, and Entry 41 of List II suggests there can be more than one State Public Service. Local authorities are included within the definition of 'State' under Article 12, Entry 5 of List II covers local authorities for local self-government, and the State is obligated to foster village panchayats under Article 40. Panchayats exercise governmental and regulatory powers, as well as taxation powers recognized by Articles 276 and 277. Under the Panchayats Act, sections 102, 122, 142, and 143 provide for officers and servants determined under section 203. Section 203 establishes a single centralized service for the entire State rather than separate services for individual panchayats. Section 206 authorizes pooling staff from different sources, including State Service; unless the Panchayat Service is a State Service, including State Service employees would be unconstitutional (State of Mysore v. H. Papanna Gowda). The statutory declaration that Panchayat Service is distinct from State Service was only intended to distinguish it from departmental services directly under State Government control and restrict transfers to panchayat posts unless promoted. Treating employees as servants of individual panchayats would lead to a bizarre change of master on every transfer. Recruitment is centralized under the Gujarat Panchayat Service Selection Board under section 210, and division into district, taluka, and local cadres does not impair its integrity as a single service. Jalgaon Zilla Parishad v. Duman Govind is distinguished because the Maharashtra statute provided for distinct services for each Zilla Parishad, whereas the Gujarat Act establishes a common service for all panchayats with the State as master.
sections.judgement: Held: (1) The Panchayat Service constituted under section 203 of the Panchayats Act has all the characteristics of a Civil Service of the State of Gujarat. This was also reflected in the State Government's resolution appointing the Second Pay Commission (Desai Commission). However, it is a question of fact to be decided in the circumstances of each case whether every employee of a Panchayat should be treated as a member of the State Civil Service. (2) Under the unamended Act, there was a common centralized Panchayat Service, as division into district, taluka, and local cadres does not affect its integrity as a single, state-wide service.
